input: This staffing review takes a closer look at the position in the quality laboratory, where a team of 16 full-time staff is responsible for handling the workload that comes through the laboratory over the course of the year. It is worth noting that overtime working has become a significant feature of the overall picture, with overtime standing at 11% of paid hours last year, reflecting the considerable pressure that is placed on the laboratory at certain times of the year and the extent to which the team has come to rely on additional hours in order to keep up with the work that is expected of it. One option that has been considered in some detail is the possibility of replacing half of the overtime with one additional hire, and it has been estimated that this would cost $72k per year on a fully loaded basis, taking into account the salary together with the associated costs of employment. On the face of it, this appears to offer a straightforward way of reducing the dependence on overtime while adding permanent capacity to the team. However, it should also be borne in mind that the overtime in question is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, whereas an additional hire would be paid for the full year, including those quieter periods of the year when the extra capacity may well not be fully utilised. This complicates the comparison considerably and underscores the need to weigh the recurring, year-round cost of the hire against a pattern of demand that is anything but even across the year, as well as the practical question of whether the work that arises outside the peaks can actually absorb the additional hours that the hire would provide.
target: Overtime in the quality laboratory is 11% of paid hours (16 full-time staff, last year). One additional hire, replacing half the overtime, costs $72k per year fully loaded. The trade-off is stated in one sentence: the hire spreads its cost evenly across the year, while the overtime it replaces is concentrated in two seasonal peaks. Fully loaded means the salary together with the costs of employing the person, and the figure is a recurring annual cost, incurred in full in quiet periods as well as at peak. The review does not compare the two costs as annual totals alone, because the totals conceal the difference that decides the question: when each cost falls. The overtime cost, by contrast, arises only when the hours are worked, so it tracks the demand pattern that causes it. Laboratory management owns the decision, and the test to apply is whether work exists outside the peaks that can be scheduled into the hired hours. If the hired hours can be filled outside the peaks with work the laboratory needs done, the hire converts a peak-only cost into year-round capacity at the stated price. If they cannot, the hire pays for idle time for much of the year, and the overtime, concentrated as it is, remains the closer match to the demand pattern. The review therefore turns on the content of the off-peak hours, not on the headline cost: the same salary is good value against a full off-peak programme and poor value against an empty one, and the laboratory's own forward work list is the evidence on which the decision should rest. Until that list is examined, the figures support neither option, and the review records the position rather than a recommendation.
